title: Rolling out a policy without an outage
summary: Audit, fix, enforce in stages.

steps.l: Install the policy in audit mode
steps.n: The rule reports violations but blocks nothing.
A policy report lists every workload that breaks the rule.
Each owner gets their findings with a fix example and a deadline.
Owners fix the manifests. A rare exception needs a reason, an owner and an end date.
Enforce mode starts where a failure costs little.
The team checks denied requests and corrects confusing messages.
Production follows once the denial rate is near zero. Exceptions expire automatically.

title: Recovering from ransomware with an immutable backup
summary: Contain, restore in order, and verify.

steps.n: Network access is cut and tokens are revoked so the attacker cannot spread or delete more.
The locked copy in the separate account shows no deletions. Retention is still enforced.
Directory and name servers are rebuilt from known good images and restored from backup.

steps.l: Restore databases to a clean point
steps.n: The restore point is chosen before the first sign of the intrusion.
Applications are deployed from trusted code, not cleaned in place.

steps.l: Verify and return users in stages
steps.n: Checks run on each stage before traffic returns. Credentials are rotated.

title: How the kernel checks a file permission
summary: Owner, group, other and the execute bit on directories.

steps.n: The program asks the kernel to open a file. The call carries the user and group ids of the process.
The kernel needs execute permission on /, /srv and /srv/app to pass through them.
The filesystem returns the owner, the group and the permission bits of data.txt.
If the user is the owner, the owner bits are used. Otherwise the group bits, otherwise the other bits.
Opening for reading needs r. Opening for writing needs w. The decision is made on that one class.

steps.l: Return a handle or an error
steps.n: A file descriptor on success, or Permission denied. SELinux can still deny after this step.

title: What happens between power on and a login prompt
summary: Firmware, boot loader, kernel and systemd.

steps.n: The firmware checks hardware and finds the boot device.
The firmware starts GRUB from the EFI partition.
GRUB loads the kernel and a small temporary filesystem with the drivers needed to find the root disk.
The kernel mounts the root filesystem and drops the initramfs.
The kernel starts systemd as the first process.
systemd starts services in dependency order until multi-user.target and the login prompt appear.

title: How a pipeline connects commands
summary: Standard output of one command becomes input of the next.

steps.l: Parse cat log | grep ERROR | wc -l
steps.n: The shell splits the line at the pipe characters into three commands.
The shell creates a pipe between each pair and starts all commands at the same time.
grep reads lines from its standard input and prints only those that contain ERROR.
Matching lines flow through the pipe to wc as they are produced.
wc -l counts the lines until the pipe closes.
Without pipefail the shell reports only the status of the last command.

title: Why quoting protects a variable
summary: Word splitting and globbing without quotes.

steps.n: The variable holds one name with a space inside.
Without quotes the shell expands the variable and then splits it on spaces.
rm receives my and report.txt as separate names and may delete the wrong file.
With quotes the expansion stays one word.
rm receives my report.txt exactly as stored.
Quote variables by default. Unquoted use is the exception.

title: How a virtual environment isolates packages
summary: Separate site-packages for each project.

steps.n: A folder is created with its own interpreter link and an empty site-packages.
The shell puts .venv/bin first in PATH, so python and pip now point there.
pip reads the active environment and installs into its site-packages.
Nothing is written to the system Python, so other projects are not affected.
The exact versions are recorded so others can rebuild the same environment.
Removing the folder and reinstalling from the file gives a clean copy.

title: Retrying a failed API call with backoff
summary: Waiting longer after each failure.

steps.n: The script sends the request with a timeout.
The server is busy. The error is temporary, so a retry is allowed.
A small random delay stops many clients from retrying at the same moment.
The script sends the same request again after the wait.
The wait grows to 2 seconds, then 4, up to a limit.
The call returns 200. If the limit is reached, the script reports the failure instead of looping forever.

title: How a TCP connection starts and ends
summary: SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK, then FIN.

steps.n: The client picks a starting sequence number and asks to connect.
The server confirms and sends its own starting number.
The client confirms. The connection is open after one and a half round trips.
Data is split into segments, numbered and acknowledged.
One side says it has finished sending.
The other side closes too. A firewall that drops these packets leaves half open connections.

title: How TLS protects an HTTPS request
summary: Certificate check and a shared key.

steps.n: The browser lists the TLS versions and ciphers it supports and the server name.
The server sends its certificate chain and chooses a cipher.
The browser checks that a trusted authority signed the certificate, the name matches and it has not expired.
Both sides compute the same session key without sending it.
Both confirm the handshake. From now on everything is encrypted.
The request and the response travel encrypted with the session key.

title: How the Docker build cache decides what to rebuild
summary: Layers are reused until something changes.

steps.n: The builder reads the Dockerfile from top to bottom.
The builder asks whether this instruction and its input files match a cached layer.
Unchanged instructions reuse the stored layer, which is almost instant.
You edit app code, so the COPY . layer no longer matches.
Every later instruction runs again, because each layer depends on the one before.
Putting rarely changed steps first keeps most of the build cached.

title: What docker compose up does
summary: Network, volumes and ordered startup.

steps.n: Compose parses services, networks, volumes and dependencies.
A project network is created. Services find each other by name.
Named volumes are created if they do not exist.
The database container starts and its health check begins.
When the check passes, services that depend on it with the healthy condition can start.
The app connects to db by name and the published port opens on the host.

title: From a pull request to production
summary: Checks, review, merge and deploy.

steps.n: The pipeline starts with lint, unit tests and scans.
Failed checks block the merge and show the log.
A reviewer reads the change and the test results.
Approval and green checks unlock the merge.
The pipeline builds one artifact and stores it with a version.
The tested artifact is promoted step by step to production with a health check.

title: How a pipeline cache speeds up builds
summary: Dependencies restored by a key.

steps.n: The key is built from the hash of the lock file, so it changes only when dependencies change.
The job asks the store for an entry with that key.
The dependencies are unpacked in seconds.
Only the project code needs work.
On a miss the job installs normally and saves the folder under the new key.
Never cache secrets or build outputs that must be fresh.

title: What happens when you create a pod
summary: API server, scheduler and kubelet.

steps.n: The request is authenticated, authorized and validated.
The pod object is saved with no node assigned.
It filters nodes by resources and rules, then scores them.
The scheduler writes the chosen node name into the pod.
The kubelet on that node pulls the image and starts the containers.
Status goes back to the API server and kubectl get pods shows Running.

title: How the horizontal autoscaler adds pods
summary: Metrics, target and replica count.

steps.n: The metrics server reports current CPU use of every pod.
Every 15 seconds the autoscaler reads the average against the target, for example 60 percent.
desired = current x (current use / target), rounded up.
The autoscaler changes the replica count within the min and max limits.
The scheduler places them if nodes have room. Otherwise a node autoscaler must add a node.
A stabilisation window avoids flapping when load drops for a short time.

title: How remote state and locking protect a team
summary: One source of truth and one writer at a time.

steps.n: Terraform starts and needs the current state.
The backend records who holds the lock. A second apply waits or fails.
The latest state is downloaded from the shared backend.
Terraform compares code, state and reality and makes the changes.
The updated state is saved with a new version.
Others can now run. Versioning allows a rollback of the state file.

title: How a module is reused
summary: One definition, many environments.

steps.n: The root passes variables such as cidr and name.
The module creates a VPC, subnets and routes using those inputs.
The provider translates resources into API calls.
The module exposes subnet ids as outputs.
Other modules receive the ids by reference.
Another call with other inputs creates a second copy without copied code.

title: How a role gives temporary access
summary: Assume role and short-lived credentials.

steps.n: The application proves its identity, for example with its instance profile.
The service verifies that this identity may assume this role.
Credentials with a short expiry are returned.
The application signs the request with the temporary keys.
The storage service checks that the role may read this bucket.
After expiry the keys stop working, so a leak has a short life.

title: What happens when a function is invoked
summary: Cold start, run and scale out.

steps.n: An event or an HTTP request arrives.
If a warm one is free, the request goes to it and no start-up cost is paid.
If none is free, a new environment is created and the code is loaded. This adds latency.
The code runs within the memory and time limits.
The response goes back. The environment stays warm for a while.
More concurrent requests create more environments, up to the account limit.

title: How a distributed trace follows a request
summary: Trace id passed from service to service.

steps.n: The first service creates a trace id and a root span.
The id travels in a request header to the next service.
Each service creates a child span and forwards the same trace id.
The payment service records a span for a 900 ms query.
Every service sends its spans to the backend in the background.
The backend joins spans by trace id and shows where the time went.

title: How logs travel from a container to a search page
summary: Collect, parse, ship and index.

steps.n: The app writes one event per line with level, message and request id.
An agent on the node reads new lines and adds labels such as pod and namespace.
Fields are parsed, noisy lines are dropped and secrets are masked.
Batches are sent with a buffer and retry, so a short outage loses nothing.
Events are indexed by time and labels, with a retention period.
An engineer searches one request id and sees all events across services.

title: How an error budget guides releases
summary: Spend, watch and decide.

steps.n: For example 99.9 percent of requests succeed over 30 days.
Monitoring computes the good request ratio all the time.
About 43 minutes of failure per month are allowed at 99.9 percent.
The team ships features at normal speed.
Releases slow down and reliability work takes priority.

steps.l: Review at the end of the period
steps.n: The team resets, learns from the burn and adjusts the SLO if needed.

title: From incident to learning
summary: Timeline, causes and follow up.

steps.n: Alerts, chat messages and deploys are put in time order.
A facilitator keeps the review blameless and focuses on systems.
The group asks why at each step until it reaches process and design gaps.
Each item has an owner, a due date and a way to check it.
Open items are reviewed weekly.
The write-up is shared, so other teams avoid the same failure.

title: What a namespace changes for a process
summary: How the kernel gives a process its own view of the system.

steps.n: The runtime asks the kernel to start a process with new pid, mount, network and hostname namespaces, using clone or unshare.
The process begins running, but the kernel gives it a separate list of process ids, mounts and network interfaces.
Inside the pid namespace the first process is pid 1, and it cannot see any process of the host in its own process list.
The network namespace has only the interfaces that were attached to it, such as one virtual interface and the loopback.
From the host the same process has a normal pid, and tools like lsns and nsenter can enter its namespaces to debug it.
nsenter runs a host tool inside the namespaces of the process, which helps when the container image has no tools of its own.

title: Memory limit versus CPU limit in a cgroup
summary: Why going over memory kills a process but going over CPU only slows it.

steps.n: The group has memory.max of 512 MB and a CPU quota of half a core, written as files under /sys/fs/cgroup.
The process has plenty of work and asks the scheduler for CPU time all the time.
After using its quota in the period, the group is paused until the next period starts, so work is spread out over more time.
cpu.stat counts throttled periods. Latency rises but nothing is killed, which makes this problem easy to miss.
Memory use reaches memory.max and the kernel cannot reclaim enough pages from the group.
The kernel kills a process in the group. The runtime reports exit code 137 and OOMKilled, and memory.events counts the kill.

title: Out of space with free space
summary: How a filesystem can refuse new files while df shows free blocks.

steps.n: The application creates a small file for each user session in one directory.
Every file needs an inode (a file record) in addition to data blocks, and the number of inodes is fixed when the filesystem is made.
Over weeks the directory holds nearly thirteen million tiny files, because the cleanup job has been failing quietly.
All inodes are used, so a new file fails with ENOSPC even though most blocks are free.
df -h shows 60 percent free, but df -i shows 100 percent of inodes used, which names the real problem.

steps.l: Remove old files, fix the job
steps.n: The operator deletes old session files, repairs the cleanup job and adds an alert on inode use.

title: How a package install is verified
summary: Why apt and dnf check signatures before installing.

steps.n: The admin asks the package manager to install a package and its dependencies.
The package manager downloads the signed list of packages and versions, named Release or repomd.
It checks the signature with the repository public key stored in the local keyring. A bad signature stops everything.
Package files are fetched, and their checksums must match the signed metadata.
The package manager compares each hash with the signed list and resolves which other packages are needed.
Files are unpacked and maintainer scripts run as root, which is why you only trust repositories you have checked.

title: How getopts reads options
summary: How a script turns -d dir -n into variables.

steps.n: The caller starts the script with short options. -d and -k take a value, and -n is a flag.
The option string lists the valid letters. A colon after a letter means that the option needs a value.
Each call sets opt to the letter and OPTARG to its value, so the case statement can copy it into a variable.
The script assigns the values to local variables and uses defaults for options that were not given.
If the caller passes -x, getopts sets opt to a question mark and the script prints usage to standard error.
The script exits with 64, the usage error convention, so callers and pipelines can tell a mistake from a failure.

title: Why "${files[@]}" matters
summary: What happens to names with spaces when expanding arrays.

steps.n: The array holds two elements. The first one contains a space.
Without quotes the shell expands the array and then splits the result on spaces, so the first name becomes two words.

steps.l: Loop sees a, b and c
steps.n: The loop body runs three times, with names that do not exist. A backup or a delete would act on the wrong things.
With double quotes each element is kept as one word, whatever characters it contains.
The loop runs twice with the real names, so the command acts on exactly the files in the array.
A careful script also compares how many items it found with how many it processed, which catches this kind of error.

title: What pipefail changes
summary: How a failure in the middle of a pipeline is noticed.

steps.n: The script downloads data and pipes it to a second command.
The server returned an error, so curl exits with a failure code and prints nothing useful.
jq gets empty input, prints nothing and exits with 0, because an empty input is valid for it.
Without pipefail the pipeline status is the status of the last command, so the script thinks all is well.
With pipefail the pipeline returns the failing status of any command in it, here the 22 from curl.
Combined with set -e, the script stops at the failed download instead of carrying on with empty data.

title: Why a script works by hand but not in cron
summary: How the cron environment differs from your login shell.

steps.n: The admin runs the script by hand. It works because the login shell has a long PATH and the right working directory.
cron runs the command with a minimal environment: a short PATH, no profile files and the home directory as the current directory.
The tool lives in /usr/local/bin which is not in cron PATH, so the script fails on its first call.
cron sends output to local mail or drops it, so nobody sees the error unless the script writes a log.
Running the script with env -i and a short PATH shows the same error in a terminal.
The admin uses full paths, sets PATH at the top, changes to the script directory and redirects output to a log file.

title: A thread pool running 100 checks
summary: How a worker limit keeps a script fast and polite.

steps.n: The script submits one task for each URL and the pool holds them in a queue.
Only max_workers tasks run at the same time, so the remote service sees at most 20 requests in parallel.
Each worker waits for its reply. While it waits it releases the interpreter lock, so other workers can run.
Results are handled as soon as each task finishes, in any order, so slow tasks do not delay fast ones.
A task that exceeds its timeout raises an error, and the script records the failure instead of stopping.
At the end the script prints how many checks failed and which ones, so nothing is lost silently.

title: asyncio with a semaphore
summary: How one thread handles many network calls at once.

steps.n: The program creates one coroutine for each URL and asks the event loop to run them all.
Each coroutine waits for the semaphore, which allows at most 50 calls at once.
A coroutine that got a slot sends its request and then yields control instead of blocking the thread.
While one call waits for the network, the loop runs another coroutine, so one thread keeps many calls in flight.
When the response comes in, the loop resumes the waiting coroutine and releases the semaphore slot.
With return_exceptions set, a failed call is returned as a value and does not cancel the others.

title: From command line to function call
summary: How argparse validates input before your code runs.

steps.n: The user types a command with a subcommand, a name and a flag.
The shell splits the line into a list of words, which becomes sys.argv in Python.
argparse finds the status subcommand, checks that the name is present and converts types such as --timeout to float.
If something is wrong, argparse prints usage and a clear message to standard error and exits with code 2.
With valid input, your function receives an object with the fields, and the code does not parse text itself.
The tool prints its result, such as JSON, to standard output and logs to standard error, and returns an exit code.

title: Reading a traceback from the bottom
summary: How to find the cause of an exception quickly.

steps.n: The script fails and Python prints a traceback with several frames.
The final line names the error and the value, for example KeyError: qty. It is the answer to what went wrong.
The line above the error shows the file and line where it happened, and the code is displayed next to it.
The frames above show how the program got there, so you can see which input led to the failing line.
The developer copies the smallest failing input into a test, which proves the bug and guards against its return.
The code is changed, for example with a default, and the test and the script now pass.

title: How a host gets an IPv6 address
summary: Router advertisements and stateless autoconfiguration.

steps.n: The interface builds an fe80:: address for itself, which works only on this network segment.
The host asks the neighbours whether anyone else uses the address, using ICMPv6 neighbour discovery.
The host asks any router on the segment to announce itself, instead of waiting for the next periodic message.
The router replies with the network prefix, usually a /64, the default route and sometimes DNS server addresses.
The host combines the prefix with an interface identifier and now has a routable address, with no server keeping a lease.
The host learns DNS servers from the advertisement or DHCPv6, and can open connections over IPv6.

title: Why a broken IPv6 path makes a site slow
summary: How clients choose between IPv6 and IPv4 and what a timeout costs.

steps.n: The browser asks for both IPv6 and IPv4 addresses of the site.
DNS returns an AAAA record and an A record, because the site was set up for both.
Clients prefer IPv6, so the first connection attempt goes to the IPv6 address.
The firewall in front of the site allows only IPv4, so the IPv6 packets are dropped and nothing comes back.
Modern clients start an IPv4 attempt after a short delay, but older ones wait for the full timeout before they try.
Users on IPv6-first networks see a delay of seconds or more. Testing with curl -6 finds the problem quickly.

title: An MTU black hole in a VPN
summary: Why small packets work and large ones hang.

steps.n: A short SSH login or a health check fits into small packets, so everything seems to work.
The server sends full-size packets of 1500 bytes with the do-not-fragment flag set.
The VPN wraps each packet in extra headers, so the usable size drops to about 1400 bytes.
A router on the path cannot forward the packet and should send back an ICMP message asking for smaller packets.
A firewall drops that ICMP message, so the server never learns that it must send smaller packets.
The server keeps resending large packets that never arrive. Lowering the MTU or clamping the MSS fixes it.

title: Why a fast link can still be slow
summary: How round trip time limits one TCP connection.

steps.n: TCP lets the sender have only a limited amount of unacknowledged data in flight, called the window.
The data crosses an ocean and takes about 75 milliseconds one way.
The sender can only send more when acknowledgements arrive, one round trip later.
With a 64 KB window and a 150 ms round trip the sender cannot exceed roughly 3.5 megabits per second.
The operator runs a single stream and then four parallel streams to see how much the window is the limit.
Use larger buffers, parallel connections, a closer endpoint or a CDN, rather than buying a bigger link.
